children: By Jack Pitcher
David Booth launched his investing firm 45 years ago, from his Brooklyn Heights apartment. It just passed $1 trillion in assets under management.

Milestones, and perhaps especially those punctuated with 13-digit achievements, can serve as a good time to reflect, says Booth, the chairman of Dimensional Fund Advisors. And Booth, who turns 80 later this year, is choosing this moment to reflect on his life and five-decade investing career in a new book, "Stay Calm: Learn to Embrace Uncertainty in Investing and Life" (Authors Equity, 220 pgs.).
The book, published Sept. 1, details Booth's early years at the forefront of the index-fund revolution. Investing, he writes, is really just a bet on human innovation-and one that is worth the risks.
In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, Booth discussed why market uncertainty is a good thing, the "miracle" of modern investing access, and why he's optimistic about the future.
WSJ: You spent decades touting passive, follow-the-market stock investing. What's it been like to watch that go from an obscure, unpopular strategy to a dominant force in U.S. investing?

DAVID BOOTH: It's been refreshing. In 1971 when I got out of school, people fought these ideas. You'd talk to fund managers or journalists, and they'd say, "You eggheads. You don't understand markets."

Still, it's not clear how many people have really got the message about how difficult the market is to beat. If you look at the growth in index funds, there's been similar growth in trading volumes. Some people are trading in and out of these, trying to time the market.
And then you've got the growth of prediction markets and all kinds of wild investing strategies. We've still got room for better investor education.
WSJ: What do you hope people take away from the book?

BOOTH: The book is not about how to invest; it's about how to think about investing. There's a lot of anxiety right now, but if people better understood how public markets work, they'd be far more likely to invest and stay invested. If there were no uncertainty, there'd be no risk, and all investments would yield the exact same riskless return. Uncertainty creates the opportunity.

The book isn't overly technical. I want it to be accessible. My parents grew up in the Great Depression and fought in World War II. They never really invested in public markets and they probably had a more difficult retirement than they should have. They viewed themselves as outsiders, and thought the insiders would take advantage of them and take all their money. And so they never invested.
Today, if you get the market return, you've done about as well as the pros. That's a miracle, I think. We ought to have a ticker-tape parade for that kind of conclusion.
WSJ: Stock indexes today have historically high concentration in megacap technology and AI stocks. Does that make you uneasy?

BOOTH: That's primarily true for the U.S. market. If you hold half your money in the U.S. and half internationally, a large part of that concentration risk goes away. As for AI, we don't know who the eventual winners will be.

Think back to the 19th-century gold rush. Who was the big winner? Levi Strauss did pretty well. It wasn't necessarily the gold miners themselves. That's why you want to buy the whole market rather than bet on individual names.
WSJ: How should investors mentally process major market panics, like the crash during the outbreak of the pandemic in 2020?

BOOTH: Every down market I've lived through over 55 years triggers the same reaction: people see the market down 20% or 30% and think, "I better get out." What we try to explain is that markets price in bad news rapidly to reach a level where expected returns are positive again.

When bad things happen to firms and individuals, they don't just sit there and take it. They figure out how to get back on track. When that ingenuity is applied, the whole economy is likely to get back on track faster than you might think.
This interview was edited and condensed for clarity.
